title: How Lasers Work
summary: Josh and Chuck give a traditional "how X works" overview of lasers. They explain how laser light differs from regular light (monochromatic, coherent, collimated), the role of Einstein's theory and stimulated emission, the early history from Charles Townes' maser to Theodore Maiman's 1960 ruby laser, and the main laser types: solid state, gas, fiber, dye, and diode (laser pointers). They cover pulsed lasers and their power, and real-world uses including barcode scanners, fiber internet, medicine (surgery, tumor treatment, dermatology, tattoo removal, LASIK), military directed-energy weapons, laser cooling and atomic clocks, and fusion research. The episode ends with a listener email about purple at a church and the sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts joke around and introduce the topic of lasers as a traditional how-it-works episode.

segments.title: What a laser is and where lasers show up
segments.summary: The laser acronym is explained and everyday examples such as supermarket UPC scanners are introduced.

segments.title: Regular light and the visible spectrum
segments.summary: White light is described as a mix of visible wavelengths, and the spectrum of colors is explained with nanometer ranges.

segments.title: Three differences of laser light
segments.summary: Laser light is described as monochromatic, coherent (in phase), and collimated (same direction).

segments.title: Einstein, photons, and the Planck relation
segments.summary: Einstein's proposal that light comes in discrete packets called photons is covered, along with the energy relation E=hf and how electrons absorb and emit photons.

segments.title: Spontaneous vs stimulated emission
segments.summary: Spontaneous emission is described, followed by stimulated emission, where one photon triggers an identical photon, creating the cascade needed for lasers.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short mid-episode break is announced.

segments.title: Charles Townes' maser and Maiman's first ruby laser
segments.summary: Charles Townes builds a microwave maser at Bell Labs, Arthur Schawlow proposes an optical version, and Theodore Maiman builds the first working laser in 1960 using a pink ruby crystal, flash coil, and silvered ends.

segments.title: Solid state lasers and gain media
segments.summary: Solid state lasers use doped crystals or glass as the gain medium, with examples including neodymium YAG and ytterbium; the gain medium is chosen for the intended application, including tattoo removal and skin treatment.

segments.title: Gas lasers
segments.summary: Gas lasers use gases such as carbon dioxide, argon, or krypton as the gain medium. Carbon dioxide lasers can weld and cut metal, and excimer lasers use UV light for tissue work without heat.

segments.title: Fiber lasers, fiber internet, and laser communication
segments.summary: Fiber lasers are described with high electricity-to-light efficiency, and laser-based fiber internet is explained. Hosts mention possible Earth-Moon laser communication.

segments.title: Dye lasers and diode laser pointers
segments.summary: Dye lasers use organic dyes as the gain medium and can be tuned to different wavelengths. Diode laser pointers are cheap and weak, and shining them at airline pilots is dangerous.

segments.title: Pulsed lasers and laser power
segments.summary: Laser power is measured in watts. Pulsing a laser concentrates energy into short bursts, which was first demonstrated in 1961 with the ruby laser.

segments.title: Pulse energy comparison
segments.summary: Giant pulses are described as building energy in very short bursts, and the discussion moves toward real-world uses.

segments.title: High-powered research lasers and laser fusion
segments.summary: The Zeus laser at the University of Michigan and the Vulcan Laser in the UK are described. Lasers are used to study extreme conditions, and Lawrence Livermore Lab achieved a net energy gain in fusion in 2022 using 192 lasers.

segments.title: Lasers in general uses
segments.summary: Hosts note lasers appear in many applications wherever light can be reflected or absorbed.

segments.title: Medical lasers: surgery, endoscopes, dermatology, LASIK
segments.summary: Lasers are used in surgery as an alternative to scalpels, including a brain tumor procedure through a small skull hole, endoscopic tumor shrinking, cosmetic dermatology, and LASIK eye surgery, which was approved in the US in 1999.

segments.title: Military laser weapons
segments.summary: The Army, Navy, and Air Force are developing directed energy laser weapons, including ship turrets that can take down drones and an Army vehicle-mounted system.

segments.title: Laser cooling and atomic clocks
segments.summary: Laser cooling uses lasers to slow and trap atoms in place, which could improve atomic clocks. The hosts link this to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.

segments.title: Listener mail: purple at a church
segments.summary: A listener explains that purple at African American church funerals may reflect royalty, Jesus Christ, or the deceased's favorite color.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener email and close the episode with iHeartRadio credits.
